# Presentations

## Three Groups {.plain-title}

::: {.steps}
1. What your backtest earned, and what you compared it against
2. What changed when you switched to `ARY` and `datekey`
3. The thing that broke
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
If your annual return went down when you fixed the point-in-time problem, that
is the most useful slide anyone will show today. Say by how much.
:::

# Stop Borrowing, Start Predicting

## What the Peer Median Assumes

::: {.lead}
That every company in an industry deserves the same multiple.
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
Two software companies, same industry. One grows at twenty percent with a forty
percent margin; the other grows at three percent and barely breaks even. The
peer median says they should trade at the same P/E, and calls the difference
mispricing.
:::

It is not mispricing. It is the model being wrong.

## The Alternative {.band-bottom}

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[Borrow a multiple]{.card-title}

Find companies that look like this one. Use the middle of what they trade at.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Predict a multiple]{.card-title}

Estimate what the market pays for growth, for profitability, for leverage. Apply
those prices to this company.
:::
:::

::: {.note}
The second one is a regression, and the first one is a special case of it --- a
regression on industry dummies and nothing else.
:::

# One Cross-Section

## Freeze a Date

::: {.lead}
One row per company, on a single day. Three thousand rows, and no time
dimension at all.
:::

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Build a cross-section as of June 30 of last year: one row per stock, with P/E
> from `daily`, and from the most recent `sf1` annual filing bring in ROE,
> revenue growth, the operating margin, leverage, and payout. Add sector.

::: {.note}
Everything today happens inside this one table. The time series comes back at
the end.
:::

## What Goes on the Left

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[P/E]{.card-title}

Bounded below at zero, unbounded above, and violently skewed. OLS on this is
mostly fitting the tail.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[log P/E]{.card-title}

Roughly symmetric. Coefficients read as percentage effects on the multiple,
which is how you want to think about them anyway.
:::
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
And the negative-earnings problem does not go away --- you cannot take the log
of a negative P/E, so those companies leave the sample. Note how many, and which
kind.
:::

## What Goes on the Right {.plain-title}

| | |
|---|---|
| Growth | Revenue growth, earnings growth --- what the multiple is supposed to be paying for |
| Profitability | ROE, ROA, margins |
| Risk | Leverage, and how variable the earnings have been |
| Size | Log market cap |
| Sector | Dummies --- which is where the peer median hides |

::: {.note}
Start with a handful you can defend. A regression with forty right-hand
variables is a machine learning problem, and that is Tuesday.
:::

## Run It

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Regress log P/E on those characteristics with sector fixed effects. Winsorize
> the right-hand variables at 1 and 99 percent. Show me the coefficients, the
> standard errors, and the R-squared.

::: {.note .note-plum}
Then read the coefficients before you look at anything else. Does the market pay
more for growth? For profitability? If a sign is backwards, that is the finding,
and it usually means a variable is built wrong.
:::

## What R-Squared to Expect

::: {.lead}
Somewhere between a third and a half. Which is enormous, and does not mean what
you want it to mean.
:::

::: {.note}
Cross-sectional valuation regressions fit well because companies genuinely do
trade on their fundamentals. The question is not whether the fit is good. It is
whether what is left over is worth trading.
:::

# Relative Value

## Fitted and Residual {.band-bottom}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Fitted]{.card-title}

What the market, on average, pays for a company with these characteristics.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Actual]{.card-title}

What this company actually trades at.
:::

::: {.card}
[Residual]{.card-title}

The gap. Negative means it trades below what its own characteristics justify.
:::
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
The residual is the signal, and it is exactly the same shape as last session's
signal --- own multiple against a predicted one. All that changed is how the
prediction is made.
:::

## Two Readings of a Negative Residual {.compare}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[It is cheap]{.eyebrow}

The market has not noticed. Buy it, wait for the gap to close.

This is the assumption the whole strategy rests on.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[Your model is missing something]{.eyebrow}

The company is in litigation, or its growth is about to stop, and the market
knows. The gap is information you failed to include.
:::
::::

::: {.note}
You cannot tell these apart for any single company. You can only find out in
aggregate, over many companies and many years, which is what the backtest is for.
:::

## Look at the Extremes

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Show me the twenty largest positive and twenty largest negative residuals,
> with their characteristics and their sector.

::: {.note .note-plum}
If the cheap list is all one sector, your sector dummies are not doing their
job. If it is all microcaps, size is entering the pricing in a way your model
has not captured. Either way you learn it in thirty seconds by looking.
:::

## Against Last Session {.plain-title}

::: {.lead}
The peer median is the same regression with only sector dummies on the right.
:::

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Fit it three ways on this cross-section: sector dummies only, characteristics
> only, and both. Compare the R-squared and the correlation between the three
> sets of residuals.

::: {.note}
If the residuals correlate at 0.9, the extra machinery is not buying you a new
signal. It is buying you the same signal with more steps.
:::

# Twenty-Five Cross-Sections

## Refit Every Year {.band-bottom}

::: {.lead}
One regression per year, using only that year's data.
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
The temptation is to fit once on everything and apply the coefficients
throughout. That uses 2024 data to price a 2004 company. It is the same
look-ahead as `MRY`, wearing a different hat, and it is harder to spot because
nothing about the code looks wrong.
:::

## The Loop

::: {.steps}
1. For each June 30 from 2001 to 2025, build the cross-section
2. Fit the regression on that year alone
3. Take the residuals
4. Sort into deciles, long the cheapest, short the most expensive
5. Hold twelve months, record the return
:::

::: {.note}
Step 2 is the only thing that changed from Tuesday. Everything else is the
backtest you already have --- which is the point of having written it as code
you can read.
:::

## Watch the Coefficients Move

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Plot each coefficient by year, with its confidence band.

::: {.note .note-plum}
The price of growth is not a constant. If a coefficient flips sign in 2009 and
again in 2021, that is worth a slide in your presentation --- and it is a reason
to be suspicious of any model that assumes the relationship is fixed.
:::

## How Many Companies Survive Each Year {.plain-title}

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> For each year, report how many stocks had all the variables and how many were
> dropped, broken out by which variable was missing.

::: {.note}
Every characteristic you add shrinks the sample, and it does not shrink it
randomly. A model that requires five years of earnings history is a model
estimated on established companies only.
:::

# Did It Pay

## Three Backtests, One Table {.band-bottom}

| | |
|---|---|
| Peer median | Tuesday's result |
| Regression residual | Today's |
| Plain P/E | No prediction at all --- just buy the low multiples |

::: {.note .note-plum}
Report the average annual return, the volatility, the t-stat, and the worst year
for all three. Same dates, same universe, same weighting, or the comparison
means nothing.
:::

## The Honest Outcome

::: {.lead}
It is entirely possible that plain P/E wins.
:::

::: {.note}
That would be a real result, and a well-known one. The elaborate model has more
ways to be wrong, more parameters to fit to noise, and a smaller sample to fit
them on. Report it if you find it.
:::

What you must not do is keep trying specifications until one of them beats the
others, and then present that one.
